articleBlocks: At first, Time and The Economist made this feel like a current-affairs board. The opening clues stay ambiguous until National Geographic gives the board a cleaner test, so this guide starts with the misleading first read, then uses the later clues to show why the final connection is narrower than the early guesses and how each clue checks that same pattern without relying on the answer reveal too early.
Cosmopolitan kept the set inside publishing, but it still felt more like famous media brands than one exact category.
National Geographic was the clue that changed that read.
It is famous, but not for the same subject area as the first two titles.
That made me stop asking what these publications cover and start asking what format they share.
Once I read them as magazine titles, the whole board stopped wobbling.
Time, The Economist, Cosmopolitan, National Geographic, and Reader’s Digest all fit naturally on the same magazine rack.
The answer was Magazines (with global readership / versions).
Reader’s Digest then worked as the clean final confirmation because it sounds much more like a magazine title than a loose media brand.
solutionNarrative: I first treated the board like a list of international media brands because Time and The Economist point strongly toward journalism, and Cosmopolitan still lives in that broad world. That read was plausible, but it stayed too wide and never explained why such different titles belonged together.

The turn came when I let National Geographic lead instead of treating it like just another famous publication. Once that clue pushed me away from subject matter and toward format, the answer became much cleaner: these are all magazine titles with broad readership, not one narrow topic family.

wordHints.Time: Time works because it is best known as a long-running weekly news magazine, which is why the first read stays inside publishing.
wordHints.The Economist: The Economist keeps the early read in journalism, but it also shows the set is not limited to one narrow topic like fashion or travel.
wordHints.Cosmopolitan: Cosmopolitan matters because it broadens the board beyond current affairs and makes a pure news-title answer feel too narrow.
wordHints.National Geographic: National Geographic is the clue that pushes the board toward magazine format instead of shared subject matter.
wordHints.Reader’s Digest: Reader’s Digest confirms the answer because it is a classic general-interest magazine title with a very specific print identity.

lessons.title: Mixed subject matter can still hide one format
lessons.body: A board can jump from politics to lifestyle to science and still be solved by the format all five clues share.

lessons.title: Let the clue that breaks topic drift lead
lessons.body: National Geographic matters because it stops the solve from being about one content area and forces you to look at publication type instead.

lessons.title: Confirm with the title that sounds most shelf-ready
lessons.body: Reader’s Digest is useful because it sounds unmistakably like a magazine title, which helps confirm the answer after the pivot.
